notes: Ruling slot 22 = Togolese Armed Forces under Eyadéma; coalition slot 13 = the RPT founded 30 Nov 1969 (MD also places RPT in 13). Olympio's banned CUT sits in slot 20 (Togolese nationalism, has starting popularity); Juvento in 18; Grunitzky's UDPT in 1. No MD sprites exist for TOG, so all icons are null.

0.name: Les Anciens d'Indochine
0.text:
Togo's soldiers learned their trade in the French colonial army in Indochina and Algeria, and the demobilised veterans who returned in the early 1960s launched the coup of January 1963. Officers such as Colonel Kléber Dadjo, who briefly headed the state in 1967, remain the most French-minded figures of the military establishment.

They see France as the guarantor of order and money, favour French advisers, bases and the CFA franc, and want a disciplined, anti-communist government. Their base is the older officer corps and veterans' associations. Their leverage lies in their ties to French military and intelligence circles.

1.name: Union démocratique des populations togolaises
1.english: Democratic Union of the Togolese People
1.text:
The UDPT was formed in 1959 by Nicolas Grunitzky's Togolese Party of Progress and the northern chiefs' party of Antoine Meatchi, and governed Togo under Grunitzky from 1963 until Eyadéma's coup of January 1967. Grunitzky died in Paris in September 1969, and on 1 January 1970 the party is suspended and its leaders in exile.

The UDPT stood for close cooperation with France, private enterprise, respect for chiefs and gradual development. Its base is the conservative notables of the centre and north and Catholic civil servants. Its leverage lies in its links with Paris and the remaining loyalty of northern chiefs.

2.name: Le Barreau de Lomé
2.text:
Lomé's lawyers, doctors and senior teachers, many trained in Paris, Dakar or Germany, form a small liberal elite. With parties suspended since 1967 and the constitution set aside, they keep alive the language of rights and constitutional rule in law offices and private clubs.

They want a return to a constitution, independent courts, freedom of the press and competitive elections, and look to Western democracies as their model. Their base is the Ewe and Mina middle class of the coast. Their leverage lies in their professional standing and in their contacts abroad, which make them useful to any government seeking respectability.

3.name: Union nationale des travailleurs du Togo
3.native_full: Union nationale des travailleurs du Togo
3.text:
The UNTT gathers the unions of dockworkers, phosphate miners, railwaymen and civil servants. After the 1967 coup it was placed under close supervision, and on 1 January 1970 the regime is pressing it to align with the new Rally of the Togolese People.

The union seeks better wages, social security and fair treatment in the phosphate mines at Hahotoé and Kpémé, and defends its independence from the state. It rejects revolutionary politics and keeps contact with Western labour internationals. Its leverage lies in the port of Lomé and the phosphate industry, the country's most valuable exports.

4.name: Les Rouges de la FEANF
4.text:
Togolese students in France, organised in the Federation of Black African Students in France, include a pro-Soviet core that reads Lenin, works with the French Communist Party and condemns the 1967 coup as a French-backed seizure of power by the military.

They call for the overthrow of the military regime, nationalisation of the phosphate mines, land reform and alignment with the socialist camp. Their base is students abroad and a few teachers at home. Their leverage lies in the ideas they carry home and in their links to communist parties and youth organisations in Europe.

5.name: Les Jeunes de Bè
5.text:
Bè, the old Ewe quarter of Lomé, has been the stronghold of opposition to every government since Olympio's death. Its young men, schoolleavers and unemployed, mix radical anti-imperialism with fierce hostility to the military regime of Gnassingbé Eyadéma.

They call for the soldiers to return to the barracks, for a people's revolution against French control and for redistribution of land and jobs. Their base is the youth of Bè and the coastal quarters of Lomé. Their leverage lies in the street: demonstrations, strikes and riots in the capital that the army must contain.

6.name: Les Vengeurs du 13 janvier
6.text:
Sylvanus Olympio, Togo's first president, was murdered on 13 January 1963 at the gates of the US embassy in Lomé. A circle of his most bitter supporters in exile in Ghana and Dahomey has never forgiven the soldiers they hold responsible, foremost Eyadéma himself.

They want revenge on the military, the restoration of Olympio's legacy and the end of French domination, and are ready to seek arms and sanctuary from any power willing to help. Their base is exiles and Ewe families in the south. Their leverage lies in conspiracy and in the cross-border networks among Ewe on both sides of the Ghana frontier.

7.name: Les Compagnons de Pya
7.text:
Around Gnassingbé Eyadéma, born in Pya in the Kabyè country, a circle of northern officers, gendarmes and security men forms the hard core of his power. They control the presidential guard, intelligence and promotions, and owe everything to their patron.

They want a strong personal regime, unconditional loyalty to Eyadéma and control of the state by northerners, and they distrust both French advisers and southern elites. They are prepared to seek arms and advice from any partner. Their base is the Kabyè soldiers who dominate the army. Their leverage lies in their grip on the means of force.

8.name: Les Libanais du Grand Marché
8.english: The Lebanese of the Grand Market
8.text:
A small Lebanese community, many of them Shia from southern Lebanon, runs shops and import houses around the Grand Marché of Lomé. They follow the work of Imam Musa al-Sadr, who founded the Supreme Islamic Shia Council in Beirut in 1969, and support his social and educational projects.

The community favours a modern, socially engaged Shia identity and keeps out of Togolese politics in exchange for security. Its base is merchants and their families. Its leverage lies in trade and credit, which give it quiet influence with officials who need imports and loans.

9.name: Les Gardiens de Kerbala
9.text:
Within Lomé's Lebanese diaspora a few devout families gather at Muharram to mourn Imam Husayn and take guidance from the senior clerics of Najaf rather than from the merchant notables. Some of their sons pursue religious studies in Iraq.

They favour strict observance, clerical authority over community life and solidarity with the Shia of Lebanon and Iraq, and distrust Western and Soviet influence alike. Their following is minimal. Their leverage lies in religious legitimacy within the diaspora and in links to clerical networks in the Middle East.

10.name: Union musulmane du Togo
10.text:
The Muslim Union of Togo serves as the official representative body of Togo's Muslims, who are concentrated in Sokodé, Bafilo and the northern towns and among traders in Lomé. Its imams and notables cooperate closely with the military government, which seeks their support in the north.

The Union preaches obedience to legitimate authority, piety and Qur'anic education, and stays away from opposition politics. It favours links with the Muslim world for scholarships and mosque funding. Its base is the Tem and other Muslim communities of the central region. Its leverage lies in its role as the regime's link to Muslim Togolese.

11.name: Les Moudjahidines du Tchaoudjo
11.text:
In Tchaoudjo, the Tem country around Sokodé, a handful of young Qur'anic students inspired by preachers from Nigeria and the Sahel dream of an Islamic state like the jihad states of the nineteenth century. They meet in small study circles beyond the reach of the established imams.

They reject the secular military regime, Christian southern elites and both Cold War blocs, and call for sharia rule. Their following is tiny and unorganised. Their leverage is negligible for now, resting only on the poverty of the north and the possibility of foreign sponsors.

12.name: Les Réformistes de Sokodé
12.text:
Young scholars returning from Al-Azhar and Arab universities to Sokodé and Lomé promote a modern, reformed Islam with Arabic schools, Muslim associations and an active role for believers in public life, against both maraboutic traditions and secular disdain.

They call for Muslim education, fair representation of the north and Muslims in the state, and moral renewal, while working within the law. Their base is educated Muslim youth and traders. Their leverage lies in the schools they found and in their links to Egypt and the Gulf, which fund scholarships and mosques.

13.name: Rassemblement du peuple togolais
13.text:
The Rally of the Togolese People was founded on 30 November 1969 by President Gnassingbé Eyadéma as the political arm of his military regime, with the young administrator Edem Kodjo as secretary-general. On 1 January 1970 it is building branches across the country to replace the parties suspended since 1967.

The RPT preaches national unity above the old north-south and party rivalries, development under military guidance and authenticity, and maintains close ties to France without formal bloc membership. Its base is civil servants, chiefs and northern communities. Its leverage lies in its monopoly of state patronage.

14.name: La Chefferie traditionnelle
14.text:
Togo's canton and village chiefs, from the Ewe kingdoms of the south to the Kabyè, Tem and Moba of the north, still govern daily life in the countryside. The military regime courts them as intermediaries and they supply the crowds for its rallies.

They defend customary land rights, the dignity of the chieftaincy and the authority of elders, and care little for the East-West quarrel. Their base is the rural population, especially in the Plateaux and northern regions. Their leverage lies in land and in their ability to mobilise villages for or against the government.

15.name: Les Nana Benz
15.text:
The Nana Benz are the wealthy market women of Lomé's Grand Marché who control the wholesale trade in Dutch wax-print cloth across West Africa, and are nicknamed for the Mercedes-Benz cars they drive. Their fortunes rival those of any minister.

They favour open trade, low duties, a stable currency and good relations with whoever holds power, and finance politicians of every camp. Their base is the network of traders and retailers stretching from Lomé to Nigeria and the Sahel. Their leverage lies in money, credit and the flow of goods through the port of Lomé.

16.name: Chambre de commerce, d'agriculture et d'industrie du Togo
16.english: Chamber of Commerce, Agriculture and Industry of Togo
16.native_full: Chambre de commerce, d'agriculture et d'industrie du Togo
16.text:
The Chamber of Commerce, Agriculture and Industry represents the French trading houses, import firms and the growing number of Togolese merchants and planters. It is the main voice of private business to the military government on 1 January 1970.

It favours free trade, low taxes, a free port in Lomé, foreign investment and limited state intervention in the economy, and is firmly pro-Western. Its base is the commercial community of the capital and the coffee and cocoa exporters of the Plateaux. Its leverage lies in tax revenue and in the trade that keeps the economy running.

17.name: Les Pêcheurs d'Aného
17.text:
Since phosphate mining at Hahotoé began in the early 1960s, the tailings dumped at Kpémé have clouded the coastal waters, while the lagoons and beaches around Aného suffer erosion. Fishermen, coastal chiefs and some teachers complain that the mines are destroying their livelihood.

They demand controls on phosphate waste, protection of fishing grounds and lagoons, and compensation for affected villages. Their base is the fishing communities of the coast between Lomé and Aného. Their leverage is small but real: the phosphates are the state's main source of revenue, and unrest near the mines is unwelcome.

18.name: Juvento
18.text:
Juvento began as the youth wing of Sylvanus Olympio's movement and broke away in 1959 as a more radical nationalist party. Its leaders were jailed under Olympio and later opposed Grunitzky; since the 1967 coup the party is suspended and its militants are watched.

Juvento calls for a socialist and non-aligned Togo, independence from French economic control, Pan-African unity and reunification of the Ewe people. Its base is young southern intellectuals, teachers and students. Its leverage lies in its ideological appeal to educated youth and its links with radical movements in Ghana and beyond.

19.name: Les Maoïstes de Lomé
19.text:
A few students and young teachers in Lomé, inspired by the Chinese Cultural Revolution and the Little Red Book, have formed reading circles that reject Soviet revisionism as firmly as French neo-colonialism.

They preach a peasant-based revolution, self-reliance and a break with both superpowers, and see the military regime as a comprador government. Their base is small, among students and a handful of workers. Their leverage lies in agitation in schools and in the attention of a regime eager to root out subversion.

20.name: Comité de l'unité togolaise
20.text:
The CUT was Sylvanus Olympio's party, which led Togo to independence in 1960 and ruled until his murder in January 1963. Suspended with all other parties since the 1967 coup, it remains the largest political force in the south, with its leaders in exile or silenced.

The CUT stands for Togolese national pride, independence from French tutelage, Ewe unity across the border with Ghana and honest civilian government. It remains suspicious of the northern-dominated army. Its base is the Ewe and Mina population of the coast and the Plateaux. Its leverage lies in its mass following and the martyr's memory of Olympio.

21.name: La Légion togolaise
21.text:
Among junior officers and former colonial soldiers, a hard core admires the discipline of the French Foreign Legion and the strongmen of Africa and Latin America. They want the army to rule permanently and remake the nation by force.

They despise politicians, civilian parties and ethnic rivalry, call for militarised youth, total order and ruthless suppression of opponents, and are hostile to communism. Their base is a small group of officers and veterans. Their leverage lies in their positions inside the army and their readiness to act if Eyadéma's regime falters.

22.name: Forces armées togolaises
22.text:
The Togolese Armed Forces have ruled Togo since Lieutenant-Colonel Gnassingbé Eyadéma seized power on 13 January 1967. The army, largely recruited among the Kabyè and other northern peoples, is the core of the regime, and Eyadéma governs as president and minister of defence.

The army promises national unity, order and development, and keeps Togo close to France while avoiding open bloc alignment. Its base is the barracks of Lomé and the northern recruiting grounds. Its leverage is total: it controls the state and has twice proved that it can overthrow civilian governments.

23.name: Le Trône de Notsé
23.text:
Notsé, the ancient walled city from which the Ewe people say their ancestors fled the tyrant king Agokoli, remains the spiritual capital of the Ewe. Its paramount chief and the court around him guard the traditions celebrated in the Agbogbo festival.

The throne's supporters want the Ewe kingdoms and chiefs to have a real place in national life, defend custom and land, and dream of a cultural union of the Ewe across the Ghana border. Their base is the Ewe villages of the Plateaux and Maritime regions. Their leverage lies in tradition and ethnic solidarity.
